fyNote: Financial year ends 31 December. IHH reports in RM million.
segmentNote: Hospitals in five home markets earn almost all revenue; Turkiye and Europe is the largest, Singapore the most profitable (AR p.218).

how.title: How IHH makes money
how.text: Revenue = patients treated (hospital stays and outpatient visits) x average bill per patient

story.scale_label: plus clinics and labs, in 10 countries

items.label: Staff costs
items.tip: Salaries for doctors, nurses and hospital staff, the biggest cost.

items.label: Medicines and consumables
items.tip: Drugs, implants, surgical supplies and other materials used on patients.

items.label: Other operating costs
items.tip: Utilities, maintenance, rent on short leases, bad debts and other running costs.

items.label: Purchases and contracted services
items.tip: Outside services such as specialists, cleaning, catering and lab work.

items.label: Depreciation and amortisation
items.tip: Wear and tear on hospital buildings and medical equipment.

items.label: Finance costs
items.tip: Interest on RM13bn of borrowings and on leases.

items.label: Tax
items.tip: Income tax, raised in 2025 by deferred tax adjustments.

items.label: Partners' share of profit
items.tip: Profit belonging to minority shareholders, for example in Fortis and Parkway Life REIT.

items.label: Profit to shareholders
items.tip: What is left for shareholders: paid as dividends or kept to grow the business.

pnl.incomeNote: Plus about RM4.57 per RM100 of revenue from other income, interest and an accounting gain from Turkiye's high inflation.

fiveYear.note: Core profit, without one-off items (RM million): 2021 1,595 · 2022 1,381 · 2023 1,280 · 2024 1,685 · 2025 1,818. Reported profit fell in 2025 because of deferred tax changes, while core profit rose 8%.

rows.name: Turkiye and Europe (Acibadem)
rows.tip: 29 hospitals in Turkiye and Europe under the Acibadem brand; the biggest market by revenue.

rows.name: Singapore (Mount Elizabeth, Gleneagles)
rows.tip: 4 premium hospitals; the highest bill per patient and the most profit.

rows.name: Malaysia (Pantai, Gleneagles, Prince Court)
rows.tip: 18 hospitals; admissions and average bills both rose in 2025.

rows.name: India (Fortis, Gleneagles)
rows.tip: 31 hospitals; IHH bought more of Fortis in 2025.

rows.name: Greater China
rows.tip: Hospitals and clinics in Hong Kong and Shanghai; still loss-making.

rows.name: Labs (diagnostic laboratories)
rows.tip: Blood tests and other lab services for hospitals and clinics.

rows.name: Parkway Life REIT
rows.tip: Owns hospital and nursing-home buildings and rents them out.

segments.note: Profit for the year by segment, before head-office costs, eliminations and the Turkiye hyperinflation adjustment (AR p.218).

assets.label: Money owed by patients and insurers

balance.note: More than a quarter of what IHH owns is goodwill: the premium it paid when buying hospital groups such as Acibadem and Fortis. Net debt including leases is 0.41 times equity (AR p.50).

cash.wfNote: Hospitals generated RM5.6bn of cash, enough to pay for RM3.7bn of new capacity, interest and dividends; acquisitions such as more of Fortis were partly funded with new borrowing.

metrics.label: Market value
metrics.plain: What the whole company costs at today's share price: RM70.1 billion.

metrics.label: P/E (FY2025 profit)
metrics.plain: You pay about RM33 for every RM1 of yearly profit. A high number means investors expect growth.

metrics.label: EPS (FY2025)
metrics.plain: Profit earned for each share you own over the year.

metrics.label: Dividend yield (FY2025 dividends)
metrics.plain: For every RM100 of shares, about RM1.3 a year comes back as cash dividends.

metrics.label: Payout ratio FY2025
metrics.plain: Of every RM100 profit, about RM44 is paid out; the rest is kept to grow.

metrics.label: Price to book
metrics.plain: The share price is 2.3 times the accounting value of what shareholders own.

metrics.label: Return on equity FY2025
metrics.plain: For every RM100 shareholders have in the company, it earned about RM7 profit last year.

metrics.label: Net margin FY2025
metrics.plain: What is left as profit for shareholders from every RM100 of revenue: RM8.16.

metrics.label: Revenue growth FY2025
metrics.plain: Revenue compared with the year before.

metrics.label: Profit growth FY2025
metrics.plain: Profit to shareholders compared with the year before.

metrics.label: Net debt
metrics.plain: Borrowings minus cash: RM13.94 billion owed to lenders after using all its cash.

metrics.label: Net gearing
metrics.plain: Net debt is 41% of shareholders' funds. Under 50% is usually seen as comfortable; above 100% means lenders fund more than owners.

metrics.label: Free cash flow FY2025
metrics.plain: Cash from operations minus spending on assets and land: RM1,875 million. Negative means it borrowed or used savings to fund growth.

metrics.label: Free cash flow yield
metrics.plain: That spare cash as a share of the company's market value.

metrics.label: EV / EBITDA
metrics.plain: A price tag that includes debt: about 15 times IHH's yearly cash earnings (EBITDA RM5.6bn as reported).

metrics.label: Core profit FY2025
metrics.plain: Profit to shareholders without one-off items such as deferred tax changes and property revaluations: up 8% (AR p.50).

drivers.evidence: Management cites ageing populations and rising lifestyle diseases as tailwinds (AR p.50, p.52)
drivers.why: Long-term demand for hospital care keeps growing.

drivers.evidence: Average bill per admission rose in every market, e.g. Malaysia RM10,667 to RM11,441 (AR p.20)
drivers.why: Higher-value treatments lift revenue per patient.

drivers.evidence: More than 1,400 operational beds added in FY2025 (AR p.51)
drivers.why: More capacity means more patients, once new wards fill up.

drivers.evidence: Bought 80% of Bayindir (Turkiye), Shrimann hospital (India) and more of Fortis (AR p.51)
drivers.why: Adds hospitals quickly, but costs cash and raises debt.

drivers.evidence: Singapore admissions fell from 61,909 to 56,385 and EBITDA from RM1,825m to RM1,666m (AR p.18, p.20)
drivers.why: Its most profitable market; Mount Elizabeth Orchard has since re-opened after renovation.

drivers.evidence: Management names medical inflation and payor (insurer) pressure as challenges (AR p.51)
drivers.why: Insurers and governments push back on price increases.

drivers.evidence: Staff costs RM9.9bn, 39% of revenue; talent shortage named as a challenge (AR p.159, p.51)
drivers.why: Nurse and doctor wages rise faster than prices in some markets.

drivers.evidence: Revenue growth was partly offset by currency translation (AR p.50)
drivers.why: Most revenue is earned outside Malaysia, so a stronger ringgit lowers reported profit.

drivers.evidence: A RM402m accounting gain from hyperinflation in 2025 (RM489m in 2024) (AR p.159)
drivers.why: Makes reported profit swing; investors focus on core profit instead.

drivers.evidence: Reported profit fell 21% on deferred tax changes; core profit rose 8% (AR p.50)
drivers.why: Explains why headline profit and the underlying business moved in opposite directions.
Moderate; leaves room for more acquisitions.

drivers.evidence: Dividend raised to 10.5 sen from 10.0 sen (AR p.51)
drivers.why: Signals confidence in steady cash flow.

drivers.evidence: About 33 times reported FY2025 profit at RM7.93 (see Valuation)
drivers.why: Investors pay a premium for a defensive, growing business; slower growth would hurt.

competitors.name: KPJ Healthcare, Sunway Healthcare, Columbia Asia
competitors.source: General market knowledge, not the report

outlook.text: Enters 2026 with positive momentum from a strong core performance in FY2025 (AR p.51).
Aims for double-digit return on equity (excluding hyperinflation and one-off items) by 2028 (AR p.51).
Plans: more capacity in existing hospitals, selective acquisitions and steady dividends (AR p.51).
Challenges named: medical inflation, insurer pressure, talent shortages, geopolitical tension and cyber threats (AR p.51, p.58).

outlookOverall.text: Management says IHH enters 2026 with positive momentum and is well placed for rising healthcare demand (AR p.51).
